hook: This file presents itself as an unfinished draft that 143 different people have scribbled footnotes on, and it reads like it: casual, sloppy, tired and occasionally rude. That looseness is deliberate, so resist the urge to read it as a badly written article. It contains a lot of profanity and a deeply uncomfortable interview with a weeping, drawing-like blue man.
whyItMatters:
This is a strong example of form carrying the anomaly. The document explains that nobody can engage with the subject sincerely, and then the document itself fails to, right down to forgotten interviews, half-remembered names and footnotes that just say they are tired too.

The effect is that the reader slowly notices the gap between a man in obvious anguish and the shrugging, joking way everyone around him writes about it.
thingsToNotice:
The interview is where the jokey surface cracks. SCP-#### says it used to be Fred Johnson, the missing homeowner, and describes something invisible scraping at him like sandpaper while his room fizzed into pieces; yet when asked whether that is why he is sad, he simply says no, having already told the D-class that the questions come nowhere near the root of it. His tears turn other people into pitiful versions of themselves, who try to comfort one another and fail.

The researcher who wrote the questions on a napkin is the coldest figure here: he brushes off the D-class's complaints, snaps at him mid-interview, and slipped in a fourth question so awful the D-class refuses to read it aloud, and we never learn what it said. Watch the footnotes too, including the one where the person first picked to do the interview panicked for reasons nobody can explain, and the closing update about a note on Fred Johnson's bathroom floor, which trails off without telling you much at all.
